sn55.21:1.4: Byūha (“cul-de-sac”) is defined in the Vinaya: “one departs the same way one enters” (Bi Pc 14:2.1.8).
sn55.21:1.13: This relates to the commonly-held idea in modern Theravada that rebirth is determined by one’s “last mind-moment” or “final thought”. This idea is incorrect on a number of grounds. First, there’s no such thing as “mind moments” in early Buddhism. Second, rebirth is determined not by “thought” (citta) but by “deed” (kamma). So it would only apply in the case of someone who was actually committing good or bad kamma at the time of death, which most people are not, like Mahānāma here; he is simply returning home. Finally, what normally prevails at the time of death is habitual kamma (like keeping precepts every day) or very strong kamma (such as attaining jhāna). In the Suttas, deathbed kamma prevails only in rare cases when someone is creating very good (MN 97:38.7) or very bad (SN 42.3:2.7) kamma at the time of death; see too the case of Sarakāni in SN 55.24:9.11 and SN 55.25:11.10.
sn55.21:3.2: There is a parallel for this simile at SN 42.6:7.1.
sn55.21:3.5: Here citta (“mind”) continues from one life to the next, in the role that viññāṇa plays elsewhere (eg. DN 28:7.13).
